questions.question: 1. Which statement best describes a linked list?

answers.a: A collection stored only in contiguous memory
answers.b: A collection of nodes connected through links or pointers
answers.c: A fixed-size collection with direct indexing
answers.d: A hierarchical structure with child nodes

explanations.a: Incorrect. Contiguous storage is associated with arrays, not a defining requirement of linked lists.
explanations.b: Correct. A linked list consists of nodes connected through links or pointers.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Direct indexed access is not a defining feature of linked lists.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A hierarchical structure with child nodes describes a tree rather than a linked list.

questions.question: 2. In a singly linked list, what does the link field of the last node normally contain?

answers.a: The address of the first node
answers.b: The address of the previous node

explanations.a: Incorrect. Linking the last node to the first creates a circular relationship.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A singly linked list stores a link to the next node, not the previous node.
explanations.c: Correct. The last node has no next node, so its link normally contains NULL.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The link field stores a node reference, not the list size.

questions.question: 3. Which is a key advantage of a linked list over a fixed-size array?

answers.a: Nodes can be added or removed without requiring one contiguous block of storage
answers.b: Every element has direct indexed access

explanations.a: Correct. Linked-list nodes can be allocated independently, so the structure can grow or shrink without requiring one contiguous block.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Linked lists do not provide direct indexed access like arrays.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Link fields require additional memory, so a linked list does not always use less memory.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A linked list does not automatically sort its elements.

questions.question: 4. What is the worst-case time complexity of searching for a value in a singly linked list containing $n$ nodes?

explanations.a: Incorrect. A search may require examining many nodes.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A singly linked list does not provide the access pattern required for logarithmic search.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A single sequential search does not require quadratic work.
explanations.d: Correct. In the worst case, all $n$ nodes may need to be examined.

questions.question: 5. Suppose `head` refers to the first node. What does `head->next` represent?

answers.a: The data in the first node
answers.b: The address of the second node
answers.c: The address of the last node

explanations.a: Incorrect. The data field and link field are separate parts of a node.
explanations.b: Correct. The `next` field of the first node stores the reference to the node that follows it.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The `next` field identifies the immediately following node, not necessarily the last node.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The `next` field stores a node reference rather than the list size.

questions.question: 6. Which operation can be performed in $O(1)$ time when a pointer to the relevant node is already available?

answers.c: Inserting a new node immediately after the referenced node
answers.d: Finding the smallest value in an unsorted list

explanations.a: Incorrect. Searching for an arbitrary value may require visiting many nodes.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Reaching a particular position generally requires traversal.
explanations.c: Correct. A constant number of pointer updates is sufficient when the insertion node is already known.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Finding the smallest value requires examining the nodes.

questions.question: 7. Consider 10 → 20 → 30 → NULL. If `head` points to 10, what value is obtained from `head->next->next`?

explanations.b: Correct. Two `next` operations move from 10 to 20 and then to 30.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Following `next` moves forward rather than back to the starting node.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The second `next` reaches a valid node before the final NULL link.

questions.question: 8. In a doubly linked list, which pair of links is normally maintained in each internal node?

answers.a: Links to the previous and next nodes
answers.b: Two links to the next node
answers.c: A link to the head and a link to the list size
answers.d: A link to the first and last nodes

explanations.a: Correct. An internal doubly linked-list node normally stores links to both its previous and next nodes.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Two next links do not provide the backward connection of a doubly linked list.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Head and list-size information are not the standard pair of links in each node.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Links to the global ends are not the standard links stored in each internal node.

questions.question: 9. Which statement distinguishes a circular singly linked list from a standard singly linked list?

answers.a: Every node has two data fields
answers.c: The last node links back to the first node
answers.d: It cannot represent an empty list

explanations.a: Incorrect. Circularity changes the linking relationship, not the number of data fields.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Circular linking does not provide indexed random access.
explanations.c: Correct. The last node links back to the first node instead of ending with NULL.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A circular-list implementation can represent an empty list.
